### M5-E01 · Index the title column

> **SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture**  
> Source: [lecture5 L273-286](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“That's a savings of almost eight times.”*, [lecture5 L297-316](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“using the index that we called title_index”*

| Topic / concepts | Difficulty | Skills | Dataset | Task type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C5.1, C5.2 | ★ | CREATE INDEX, EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN | `movies` | change the database |

First run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM "movies" WHERE "title" = 'Cars';` and note the word **SCAN**.
Then create an index named `title_index` so that the plan becomes a **SEARCH** using that index.

<details><summary>Expected output (try first!)</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM "movies" WHERE "title" = 'Cars'`

```text
SEARCH movies USING INDEX title_index (title=?)
```

</details>

### M5-E02 · Which columns should be indexed for the Tom Hanks query?

> **SOURCE · question posed in the lecture**  
> Source: [lecture5 L405-447](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“Perhaps two separate indexes.”*, [lecture5 L338-348](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“will automatically create an index via which I can search for a primary key”*

| Topic / concepts | Difficulty | Skills | Dataset | Task type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C5.2 | ★★★ | EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, choosing index columns | `movies` | change the database |

Run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on the Tom Hanks query (M1-E22). Two tables are **scanned**.
Create one index per scanned table (`name_index` on people, `person_index` on stars) so that **neither table is scanned**.

<details><summary>Expected output (try first!)</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT "title" FROM "movies" WHERE "id" IN (SELECT "movie_id" FROM "stars" WHERE "person_id" = (SELECT "id" FROM "people" WHERE "name" = 'Tom Hanks'))`

```text
SEARCH movies USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?) | LIST SUBQUERY 2 | SEARCH stars USING INDEX person_index (person_id=?) | SCALAR SUBQUERY 1 | SEARCH people USING COVERING INDEX name_index (name=?)
```

</details>

### M5-E03 · Make the stars index covering

> **SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture**  
> Source: [lecture5 L499-542](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“Now I have two covering indexes.”*, [lecture5 L482-496](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“It's one in which the query data can be found only by searching the index.”*

| Topic / concepts | Difficulty | Skills | Dataset | Task type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C5.3 | ★★★ | multi-column index, covering index | `movies` | change the database |

The plan still says `SEARCH stars USING INDEX person_index`, which means SQLite looks up each matching row in the table to get `movie_id`.
Replace `person_index` with a two-column index so that `stars` is searched with a **covering index**.

<details><summary>Setup the checker runs first</summary>

```sql
CREATE INDEX "person_index" ON "stars" ("person_id");
CREATE INDEX "name_index" ON "people" ("name");
```
</details>

<details><summary>Expected output (try first!)</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT "title" FROM "movies" WHERE "id" IN (SELECT "movie_id" FROM "stars" WHERE "person_id" = (SELECT "id" FROM "people" WHERE "name" = 'Tom Hanks'))`

```text
SEARCH movies USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?) | LIST SUBQUERY 2 | SEARCH stars USING COVERING INDEX person_index (person_id=?) | SCALAR SUBQUERY 1 | SEARCH people USING COVERING INDEX name_index (name=?)
```

</details>

> **SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture**  
> Source: [lecture5 L892-924](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“Now though I'm using 1998, which were rows that were not”*

| Topic / concepts | Difficulty | Skills | Dataset | Task type |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Users mostly search this year's movies. Create a **partial** index named `recents` on `movies(title)` that only includes rows from **2023**.


```text

```

</details>

### M5-E06 · Alice pays Bob $10, atomically

> **SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture**  
> Source: [lecture5 L1201-1230](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“So this is the atomicity part of transactions.”*

| Topic / concepts | Difficulty | Skills | Dataset | Task type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C5.7 | ★★ | BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT | `bank` | change the database |

### M5-E07 · Roll back a transfer that breaks a constraint

> **SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture**  
> Source: [lecture5 L1309-1325](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“ROLLBACK like this, hit Enter”*, [lecture5 L1292-1296](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“A rollback only works while we're inside of a transaction.”*

| Topic / concepts | Difficulty | Skills | Dataset | Task type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C5.7 | ★★★ | ROLLBACK, CHECK constraint | `bank` | change the database |

Alice now has $0 and Bob has $30. Run the same transfer of $10 from Alice to Bob in a transaction.
The debit violates `CHECK("balance" >= 0)`, so undo the whole transaction so that nobody ever sees Bob at $40.
(In this exercise, statements keep running after an error, just like typing them one by one in the shell.)

<details><summary>Setup the checker runs first</summary>

```sql
UPDATE "accounts" SET "balance" = 0 WHERE "id" = 1;
UPDATE "accounts" SET "balance" = 30 WHERE "id" = 2;
```
</details>

<details><summary>Expected output (try first!)</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT * FROM "accounts"`

| id | name | balance |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Alice | 0 |
| 2 | Bob | 30 |
| 3 | Charlie | 30 |

</details>

### M5-E12 · Walk the B-tree to find Turning Red

> **SOURCE · question posed in the lecture**  
> Source: [lecture5 L782-809](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“How could I find Turning Red?”*, [lecture5 L624-648](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“I've broken that relationship”*, [lecture5 L848-861](../../sources/lecture5.txt) *“So these trade-offs are something you should”*

| Topic / concepts | Difficulty | Skills | Dataset | Task type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C5.4 | ★★ | B-tree search, index trade-offs | `movies` | self-check (not auto-graded) |

The lecture's index on `title` is a small B-tree: the root node holds **Frozen | Soul**,
and its three leaf nodes hold *Cars, Cars 3, Frozen* · *Luca, Ratatouille, Soul* · *Toy Story, Turning Red, WALL-E*.
1. List the comparisons SQLite makes to find **Turning Red**, and say what it gets back from the index.
2. Why can't SQLite simply sort the `title` column of the table itself?
3. Name the two costs you pay for this index.
